2: name: fr
3: description: Use fr for bounded inspection, structural edits, history, Git patches, checks, and Lean evidence.
4: ---
5: # Work with fr
6: 
7: Run at the root or pass `-C`. Request source only when needed:
8: ```sh
9: fr project find greet --signature
10: fr project select greet render validate --signature --source --bytes 2048
11: fr project map --depth 2 --limit 12
12: ```
13: Read coverage, omissions, pages and selection statuses. Missing or clipped rows do not prove absence.
14: Retain bases; stale identities refuse.
15: 
16: Load only the needed route: [Task](references/task.md), [Explore](references/explore.md),

22: 
23: Author with handles; refactor with names or positions. Preview mutations. Save coordinated
24: changes as one transaction, then apply it. Preserve refusals, gaps and uncertainty.

{"text": "1: # Run declared checks
2: 
3: Review the listing, then run task-relevant names with its basis:
4: ```sh
5: fr checks
6: fr checks --run unit --basis '<CHECK_BASIS>' --quiet-success --no-declarations --output-bytes 2048
7: fr checks --run unit --basis '<CHECK_BASIS>' --record-for '<TX>' --quiet-success
8: ```
9: `unit` is an example. Listing executes nothing. Runs use declared argv, directory, inherited environment, and timeout. A full basis or 32-character prefix works.
10: 
11: Read `passed`, results, `not_run`, `source_snapshot_stable`, and `configuration_stable`; null means nothing ran. Quiet success retains stream byte counts, while failures keep bounded diagnostics. `--no-declarations` requires the retained matching listing.
12: 
13: Source or configuration drift fails. `--record-for` preflights an applied transaction and attaches a source-bound receipt; required checks bind exact configuration and ordered names. Commands run without a file lock. Unsupported files, syntax acceptance, coverage labels, or unrelated checks do not establish behavior.
", "total_lines": 13, "next_line": null}

{"text": "1: # Explore only the needed structure
2: 
3: ```sh
4: fr project explore greet --in app.py
5: fr project explore greet --mode behavior --target '<HANDLE>'
6: fr project select greet render validate --signature --source --bytes 2048
7: fr project show '<HANDLE>'
8: fr project show '<HANDLE>' --relations --limit 8
9: fr project show '<HANDLE>' --source --bytes 256
10: fr project calls '<HANDLE>' --direction incoming --limit 8
11: fr project tests app.py --limit 8
12: fr project features --limit 12
13: fr project technologies --limit 13
14: fr project styles --limit 12
15: fr project diagrams --limit 12
16: fr project gaps --limit 8
17: ```
18: 
19: When the task only needs several read views, use the bounded manifest in [Batch](batch.md).
20: When those views select structural edit targets and declared checks, use [Task](task.md).
21: Keep the cache enabled. Cold calls may emit `indexing` progress on stderr; stdout remains the report.
22: 
23: For behavior discovery, start with one `project explore TERM [--contains]`. It returns no source in
24: names mode and caps the page at twelve rows. Execute the selected row's `next.arguments` exactly to
25: obtain its bounded source and direct relationships. Execute truncation continuations instead of
26: raising limits. Use `--profile expanded` only through the reported explicit expansion action.
27: 
28: When two stages are known, put `explore` requests in one `project batch --profile compact`
29: manifest and reference the selected handle through `/rows/0/handle`. This reuses one project
30: snapshot and enforces an aggregate report budget. Independent cold processes coalesce identical
31: resolution work.
32: 
33: Use exact `project find NAME` for known declarations. `--contains` is a boolean literal-substring flag.
34: Use `project select SELECTOR...` for several exact names or handles under one revision and budget.
35: Read every selector status before claiming absence. Handles can report `outside-scope`,
36: `not-a-declaration` or an omitted local; stale handles refuse instead of becoming names.
37: Use maps when hierarchy matters. Choose `<HANDLE>` from a declaration row. Full handles include their source revision.
38: Alternatively use a short ID with the returned `--revision`; never reuse a bare ID across revisions.
39: `show` gives the declaration's `position`, a 1-based line and column suitable for a refactoring target.
40: Its syntax header can contain defaults and attributes; it is not a complete semantic contract.
41: 
42: Request `--source` only when needed. Source offsets count bytes from the selected node's start, not lines or file-relative offsets.
43: For another slice, pass the returned `next_offset` with `--offset`; this preserves UTF-8 boundaries.
44: For another result page, reuse the same query and fields with `--cursor` and the returned `page.next`.
45: Changing source, manifests, scan options or query scope can invalidate a handle or cursor. Restart the relevant map or query after a stale response.
46: 
47: Maps show lexical containment, not inferred architecture.
48: Call results preserve confidence and unresolved or dispatch-candidate rows; candidates do not establish runtime dispatch.
49: Test associations are candidates for selecting checks, not proof of complete coverage or commands to execute blindly.
50: Use `project packages`, `dependencies`, `links` and `workspaces` for manifest declarations and local relationships when package boundaries matter.
51: Use `project routes`, `contracts` and `configuration` for their supported declaration patterns when the task needs those views.
52: Use [Surfaces](surfaces.md) for framework, style and embedded-diagram discovery, exact surface edits,
53: or the cross-stack Merkle view.
54: These commands do not establish complete dependency resolution or framework semantics.

{"text": "1: # Prepare one structural task
2: 
3: Use one `project task` call when an edit needs several project views, exact targets and declared
4: delivery checks. The manifest runs ordinary read-only project queries on one revision. Later query
5: arguments can reference earlier string results as described in [Batch](batch.md). Each target then
6: names a full handle directly or references a returned query report.
7: 
8: ```json
9: {
10:   "schema": "fr-project-task-1",
11:   "requests": [
12:     {"id": "target", "arguments": ["find", "render", "--signature", "--source", "--bytes", "2048"]},
13:     {"id": "callers", "arguments": ["calls", {"request": "target", "pointer": "/rows/0/0"}, "--direction", "incoming"]}
14:   ],
15:   "targets": [
16:     {"id": "render-body", "handle": {"request": "target", "pointer": "/rows/0/0"}, "op": "replace-body"}
17:   ],
18:   "checks": ["unit"],
19:   "delivery": {"exercise-reversal": true, "patch": "artifacts/change.patch"}
20: }
21: ```
22: 
23: Run `fr project task --from '<TASK_MANIFEST>'`. Read every nested query’s gaps and omissions. A
24: target’s `target-supported` eligibility only proves that its language and declaration kind can
25: enter that authoring route. It does not validate fragment bytes or the exact syntax container.
26: 
27: An `edit-body-scalar` target carries
28: `"scalar":{"operation":"set-int","from":"1","to":"2"}` and needs no fragment. Task change
29: validates its unique role match and generated intent during preview. Other authoring targets retain
30: their existing fragment rules.
31: 
32: An `edit-body-disclosed` target carries
33: `"disclosed":{"edit":"frde1:<DIGEST>","to":"7"}` and the full handle returned with that
34: capability. It needs no fragment or scalar object. Project task preserves the request in its author
35: template; task change rebinds it to the current typed body and refuses stale or changed input.
36: 
37: An `edit-body-disclosed-ir` target carries
38: `"disclosed_ir":{"edit":"frdi1:<DIGEST>","value":<TYPED_IR_NODE>}`. Omit `value` only for a
39: delete capability. Its opaque ID fixes replacement category or statement position, so do not add a
40: path or index. The Python SDK's `DisclosedIrEditRequest` emits this object from ordinary typed IR
41: constructors.
42: 
43: Write each required fragment outside recognized source. Replace every `<FRAGMENT:ID>` in
44: `author_manifest_template` with the actual path and save the result. Follow `next`: preview the
45: author batch, save it under the complete `plan_context_basis`, replace the
46: transaction placeholders in `workflow_manifest_template`, preview the workflow, and write it under
47: the complete `workflow_basis`.
48: 
49: Do not pass either template directly to its command. Preserve full bases until their reviewed
50: write. If no `.fr/checks.json` exists, omit `checks` and `delivery`; use the manual author/history
51: route and independent validation. A task reference to an omitted query report refuses, so increase
52: `--report-bytes` or narrow that query instead of guessing its handle.
53: 
54: When concrete fragments and declared checks exist, use `task-change` to remove the template joins.
55: Keep the same requests and targets, add each fragment path as target `from`, add exact author
56: `postconditions`, and use schema `fr-task-change-1`. Put `check-output-bytes` inside `delivery`.
57: 
58: Preview with `fr task-change --from '<TASK_CHANGE_MANIFEST>'`. Retain the complete diff and
59: `task_change_basis`. Execute with `fr task-change --from '<TASK_CHANGE_MANIFEST>' --write --basis
60: '<TASK_CHANGE_BASIS>'`. The second call recomputes all inputs, records one check-bound transaction,
61: and runs the requested reversal and patch lifecycle. Changed source, fragments, checks or delivery
62: choices refuse before persistence. A failed stage withholds the patch and reports its current state.
", "total_lines": 62, "next_line": null}

{"text": "1: # Author selected code
2: 
3: `fr author` changes bodies, semantic deltas, scalar plans, Rust declarations and imports. Batches
4: accept up to 32 disjoint steps. Coordinate callers after signature changes.
5: 
6: Use `fr author guide` for machine-readable operations, limits and transitions.
7: 
8: For several declarations, use one `project select NAME... --source`; duplicate names
9: across files return together. Use `project find NAME --in FILE --source` for one declaration;
10: `root` is its file handle. A module/trait row selects that container; a direct method selects
11: its impl/trait.
12: 
13: Fragments fit 64 KiB. Steps need `op` and `handle`; fragment steps add `from`.
14: `edit-body-scalar` adds `scalar` with `operation`, `from` and `to`.
15: `edit-body-disclosed` adds `disclosed: {edit,to}` and uses its paired full handle.
16: `edit-body-disclosed-ir` adds `disclosed_ir: {edit,value?}`; typed replacement/insertion values are
17: inline and deletions omit `value`. Both capability routes use their paired full handle. Short IDs
18: need top-level `revision`; `organize-imports` takes a file handle. Steps use original source; overlaps refuse.
19: Optional postconditions cover changed files, edits, operations and paths. Fragment
20: paths can be project-relative or absolute.
21: 
22: Review diff and retain `plan_context_basis`. Repeat it with
23: `--save-plan --plan-basis BASIS`; drift or clipping refuses before persistence. The result's
24: `transaction_context_basis` compacts forward application. `plan_context_basis` starts with
25: `frpb1`; `frcb1` is a project basis and cannot save a plan.
26: 
27: Rust insertion preserves bytes and docs; only traits allow bodyless functions. Body replacement
28: covers Rust, Go, Java, Python and supported JavaScript/TypeScript/TSX bindings; arrows may change form.
29: Python fragments are relative suites and cover decorated synchronous or asynchronous handlers.
30: For source-free body replacement and smaller checked changes, use [Semantic](semantic.md).
31: 
32: ```rust
33: /// Calls increment twice.
34: pub fn increment_twice(value: u32) -> u32 { increment(increment(value)) }
35: ```
36: 
37: Use the lookup's file-scoped `root` as `<FILE_HANDLE>`:
38: ```sh
39: fr project find increment --in src/lib.rs --source --bytes 512
40: fr author batch --from '<MANIFEST>'
41: fr author batch --from '<MANIFEST>' --save-plan --plan-basis '<PLAN_CONTEXT_BASIS>'
42: fr history apply '<AUTHOR_TX>' --write --no-diff --context-basis '<TRANSACTION_CONTEXT_BASIS>'
43: ```
44: Continue source with `next_offset`. Run [checks](checks.md); retain the transaction for [history](history.md) and [patch export](git.md).
", "total_lines": 44, "next_line": null}

{"text": "1: # Deliver one verified transaction
2: 
3: Use this route after reviewing and saving one complete change plan. First list `fr checks`. Retain
4: its basis, the transaction ID and the plan's `transaction_context_basis`. Write an extensionless
5: control manifest outside recognized source so creating it does not stale the plan.
6: 
7: ```sh
8: fr workflow --from '<WORKFLOW_MANIFEST>'
9: fr workflow --from '<WORKFLOW_MANIFEST>' --write --basis '<WORKFLOW_BASIS>'
10: ```
11: 
12: The schema-one manifest names `transaction`, `transaction-context-basis`, and `checks` with `basis`
13: and `names`. Optional `exercise-reversal` checks apply, undo and redo states in order. Optional
14: `patch.output` creates a new relative Git patch only after all stages pass. `check-output-bytes`
15: bounds retained failure streams.
16: 
17: Review the preview's stage list, full resolved bases, check coverage, patch digest and destination.
18: Copy its `workflow_basis` into the write. This omits that unchanged preflight envelope.
19: A failed stage stops later work and leaves their status `pending`. Inspect `transaction_status` and
20: preserve check diagnostics. A pending transaction still requires the separate recovery route.
21: 
22: This workflow checks only project-declared commands. Independent behavior oracles and receiver
23: checks remain separate evidence when the task requires them. Use the manual Checks, History and Git
24: routes when no check configuration exists or when each transition needs external validation.
", "total_lines": 24, "next_line": null}

{"text": "1: # Apply or reverse source history
2: 
3: ```sh
4: fr history show '<TX>'
5: fr history undo '<TX>'
6: fr history undo '<TX>' --write --no-diff
7: fr history redo '<TX>'
8: fr history redo '<TX>' --write --no-diff
9: ```
10: Preview transitions. `--no-diff` retains outcomes and metadata. A complete author plan's `transaction_context_basis` is `context_basis` in detailed history. Forward apply/redo may reuse it to omit reviewed diffs; undo needs full review.
11: 
12: Transitions verify affected content, links, kinds, existence, and regular-file modes while preserving unrelated files and the Git index. Undo must be latest; redo must be next; a new applied transaction abandons redo. Preserve conflicting edits.
13:

This crate provides a robust regular expression parser.

This crate defines two primary types:

* [`Ast`](ast::Ast) is the abstract syntax of a regular expression.
  An abstract syntax corresponds to a *structured representation* of the
  concrete syntax of a regular expression, where the concrete syntax is the
  pattern string itself (e.g., `foo(bar)+`). Given some abstract syntax, it
  can be converted back to the original concrete syntax (modulo some details,
  like whitespace). To a first approximation, the abstract syntax is complex
  and difficult to analyze.
* [`Hir`](hir::Hir) is the high-level intermediate representation
  ("HIR" or "high-level IR" for short) of regular expression. It corresponds to
  an intermediate state of a regular expression that sits between the abstract
  syntax and the low level compiled opcodes that are eventually responsible for
  executing a regular expression search. Given some high-level IR, it is not
  possible to produce the original concrete syntax (although it is possible to
  produce an equivalent concrete syntax, but it will likely scarcely resemble
  the original pattern). To a first approximation, the high-level IR is simple
  and easy to analyze.

These two types come with conversion routines:

* An [`ast::parse::Parser`] converts concrete syntax (a `&str`) to an
[`Ast`](ast::Ast).
* A [`hir::translate::Translator`] converts an [`Ast`](ast::Ast) to a
[`Hir`](hir::Hir).

As a convenience, the above two conversion routines are combined into one via
the top-level [`Parser`] type. This `Parser` will first convert your pattern to
an `Ast` and then convert the `Ast` to an `Hir`. It's also exposed as top-level
[`parse`] free function.


# Example

This example shows how to parse a pattern string into its HIR:

```
use regex_syntax::{hir::Hir, parse};

let hir = parse("a|b")?;
assert_eq!(hir, Hir::alternation(vec![
    Hir::literal("a".as_bytes()),
    Hir::literal("b".as_bytes()),
]));
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```


# Concrete syntax supported

The concrete syntax is documented as part of the public API of the
[`regex` crate](https://docs.rs/regex/%2A/regex/#syntax).


# Input safety

A key feature of this library is that it is safe to use with end user facing
input. This plays a significant role in the internal implementation. In
particular:

1. Parsers provide a `nest_limit` option that permits callers to control how
   deeply nested a regular expression is allowed to be. This makes it possible
   to do case analysis over an `Ast` or an `Hir` using recursion without
   worrying about stack overflow.
2. Since relying on a particular stack size is brittle, this crate goes to
   great lengths to ensure that all interactions with both the `Ast` and the
   `Hir` do not use recursion. Namely, they use constant stack space and heap
   space proportional to the size of the original pattern string (in bytes).
   This includes the type's corresponding destructors. (One exception to this
   is literal extraction, but this will eventually get fixed.)


# Error reporting

The `Display` implementations on all `Error` types exposed in this library
provide nice human readable errors that are suitable for showing to end users
in a monospace font.


# Literal extraction

This crate provides limited support for [literal extraction from `Hir`
values](hir::literal). Be warned that literal extraction uses recursion, and
therefore, stack size proportional to the size of the `Hir`.

The purpose of literal extraction is to speed up searches. That is, if you
know a regular expression must match a prefix or suffix literal, then it is
often quicker to search for instances of that literal, and then confirm or deny
the match using the full regular expression engine. These optimizations are
done automatically in the `regex` crate.


# Crate features

An important feature provided by this crate is its Unicode support. This
includes things like case folding, boolean properties, general categories,
scripts and Unicode-aware support for the Perl classes `\w`, `\s` and `\d`.
However, a downside of this support is that it requires bundling several
Unicode data tables that are substantial in size.

A fair number of use cases do not require full Unicode support. For this
reason, this crate exposes a number of features to control which Unicode
data is available.

If a regular expression attempts to use a Unicode feature that is not available
because the corresponding crate feature was disabled, then translating that
regular expression to an `Hir` will return an error. (It is still possible
construct an `Ast` for such a regular expression, since Unicode data is not
used until translation to an `Hir`.) Stated differently, enabling or disabling
any of the features below can only add or subtract from the total set of valid
regular expressions. Enabling or disabling a feature will never modify the
match semantics of a regular expression.

The following features are available:

* **std** -
  Enables support for the standard library. This feature is enabled by default.
  When disabled, only `core` and `alloc` are used. Otherwise, enabling `std`
  generally just enables `std::error::Error` trait impls for the various error
  types.
* **unicode** -
  Enables all Unicode features. This feature is enabled by default, and will
  always cover all Unicode features, even if more are added in the future.
* **unicode-age** -
  Provide the data for the
  [Unicode `Age` property](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-24.html#Character_Age).
  This makes it possible to use classes like `\p{Age:6.0}` to refer to all
  codepoints first introduced in Unicode 6.0
* **unicode-bool** -
  Provide the data for numerous Unicode boolean properties. The full list
  is not included here, but contains properties like `Alphabetic`, `Emoji`,
  `Lowercase`, `Math`, `Uppercase` and `White_Space`.
* **unicode-case** -
  Provide the data for case insensitive matching using
  [Unicode's "simple loose matches" specification](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr18/#Simple_Loose_Matches).
* **unicode-gencat** -
  Provide the data for
  [Unicode general categories](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-24.html#General_Category_Values).
  This includes, but is not limited to, `Decimal_Number`, `Letter`,
  `Math_Symbol`, `Number` and `Punctuation`.
* **unicode-perl** -
  Provide the data for supporting the Unicode-aware Perl character classes,
  corresponding to `\w`, `\s` and `\d`. This is also necessary for using
  Unicode-aware word boundary assertions. Note that if this feature is
  disabled, the `\s` and `\d` character classes are still available if the
  `unicode-bool` and `unicode-gencat` features are enabled, respectively.
* **unicode-script** -
  Provide the data for
  [Unicode scripts and script extensions](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr24/).
  This includes, but is not limited to, `Arabic`, `Cyrillic`, `Hebrew`,
  `Latin` and `Thai`.
* **unicode-segment** -
  Provide the data necessary to provide the properties used to implement the
  [Unicode text segmentation algorithms](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/).
  This enables using classes like `\p{gcb=Extend}`, `\p{wb=Katakana}` and

* **arbitrary** -
  Enabling this feature introduces a public dependency on the

/// Escapes all regular expression meta characters in `text`.
///
/// The string returned may be safely used as a literal in a regular
/// expression.
pub fn escape(text: &str) -> String {
    let mut quoted = String::new();
    escape_into(text, &mut quoted);
    quoted
}

/// Escapes all meta characters in `text` and writes the result into `buf`.
///
/// This will append escape characters into the given buffer. The characters
/// that are appended are safe to use as a literal in a regular expression.
pub fn escape_into(text: &str, buf: &mut String) {
    buf.reserve(text.len());
    for c in text.chars() {
        if is_meta_character(c) {
            buf.push('\\');
        }
        buf.push(c);
    }
}
